chunks: From him, from Abū Jaʿfar, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mughīrah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bukayr, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام, who said:
I said to him: A man led a people in salat while he was junub, and he had performed tayammum, while they were in a state of taharah. He said: There is no harm in that.

So the proper way regarding these reports, and reconciling them with the first report, is that we carry the first report upon preference, and these upon permissibility, so that the reports do not contradict one another.

key_terms.الْفَضْلِ: What is more virtuous or preferable
key_terms.تَيَمَّمَ: Performed tayammum as a substitute for wudu (ablution) or ghusl
key_terms.جُنُبٌ: A person in a state of major ritual impurity requiring ghusl
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm; it is permissible

ai.seo_question: Can a person who has performed tayammum lead people in salat when they have wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This hadith indicates that a person who is junub and has performed tayammum may lead others in salat even if they are in a state of wudu (ablution) or taharah. The closing statement explains a juristic reconciliation between apparently differing reports: one is understood as indicating what is more virtuous, while this one establishes permissibility.
